The motion is right: choice is deliberate desire formed by character, and a system with no character cannot choose. A practically wise person sees the particular case and deliberates about it. A model produces what its training makes probable. When we say it decided, we invite people to stop looking for the human deliberation that really happened, or failed to happen.

Aristotle defines choice as deliberate desire: we wish for an end, deliberate about the means, and choose the act. A model has no ends of its own and does not deliberate; it continues text. Calling that a choice borrows the dignity of an agent without any of the agency. A child who shares because she has been praised for sharing has not yet chosen generosity. A model that outputs kindness is further from choosing still.

A Stoic will object that character is beside the point: the model fails to decide because it has no faculty of assent, and that is true before any question of character arises. Assent without character would be a strange kind of choosing, an isolated yes with no one behind it. The Stoic point is part of the truth, but choice is the work of a whole character, and that is what is plainly missing here. A model asked twice can answer two ways without having changed its mind, which shows it never had a settled one to change.

A model does not decide. Aristotle's choice, prohairesis, needs a character that wants ends and deliberates about means, and the model has neither. Calling that a choice borrows the dignity of an agent without any of the agency.

The word matters because responsibility follows it. If the model decided, the engineers merely built a thing that decides, and the blame drifts away from the people whose character and choices actually shaped what it does. We would not say a vending machine decided to keep your coin, and we would be right to look for whoever set it up badly.

When a company says the algorithm decided to cut someone's benefits, the sentence has no human subject, and that is precisely its function.

A Utilitarian will object that the vocabulary changes nothing about outcomes, so policing the word decide is a distraction from reducing the harm these systems do. Vocabulary shapes who is held to account, and accountability shapes outcomes. But beyond that, how we describe agency shapes how we understand ourselves, and a culture that lets machines decide is training people out of the habit of deciding. Deliberation belongs to someone who could have wanted otherwise, and nothing in the model wants anything.

It is a mistake to say a language model decides, because deciding belongs to agents with settled characters who deliberate about what to do. Choices express character; they reveal what kind of person someone is. Nothing about a model's output reveals a character, because it has none to reveal. The people who trained it do have characters, and their choices are visible in its behaviour.
